idiom_name: SQLAlchemy declarative single table inheritance (polymorphic_on / polymorphic_identity)
implementation_notes: SQLAlchemy's declarative ORM maps single table inheritance directly: the base class declares the shared __tablename__ plus __mapper_args__ = {'polymorphic_on': <discriminator column>, 'polymorphic_identity': <base value>}, and each subclass adds only its own columns with a unique polymorphic_identity; a query on the base class then returns instances of the right subclass, and the session/identity map replaces the hand-written mapper entirely. Subclass columns live in the same table and must be nullable or server-defaulted, and sibling subclasses that want the same column name need use_existing_column. Without an ORM the same mapping is written over sqlite3/psycopg with dataclasses and a factory keyed on the type column - and note that Django's model inheritance is not STI (multi-table inheritance joins per parent, abstract bases create no table).
pitfalls: A discriminator value with no mapped class makes rows unloadable: the type column is data the mapper trusts, so adding a subtype is a schema/data change as well as a new class.
Subclass columns must be nullable (or carry defaults) and sibling columns with the same name need use_existing_column, otherwise SQLAlchemy raises a conflict or emits duplicate columns.
Django's multi-table inheritance is a different storage strategy (a join per parent), so an STI design ported from SQLAlchemy/Rails silently acquires joins.
Polymorphic loads add a discriminator predicate to every query; a query written with raw SQL or a Core select bypasses the ORM's identity handling and can return base-class objects for subclass rows.
